title: Canon Episcopi: Church Denies Reality of Night Flight with Diana
description: The Canon Episcopi, attributed to the Council of Ancyra (314 CE) but actually dating to around 906 CE when it appeared in Regino of Prüm's De Ecclesiasticis Disciplinis, declared that women who believed they rode at night with the goddess Diana were victims of demonic illusion, not actual physical night-riders. The canon authoritatively stated that such beliefs were foolish errors, that the devil deceived women into thinking they had physically traveled when they had not, and that claiming such nocturnal journeys were real was heretical. This text became the foundational skeptical document in the witchcraft debate: later demonologists like Sprenger and Kramer had to systematically argue against it to justify prosecuting night-flying witches. The Canon Episcopi established a default ecclesiastical skepticism about witch assemblies that persisted until demonologists overcame it in the fifteenth century.
historiographical_note: The Canon Episcopi is central to Norman Cohn's Europe's Inner Demons (1975), which argued that witch beliefs were fundamentally elite fantasies rather than folk realities. The canon's long history of misattribution (it was falsely dated to 314 CE) and its strategic use by both skeptics and believers makes it a key text for understanding how historical authority was deployed in the witchcraft debate.
source_method: Regino of Prüm, De Ecclesiasticis Disciplinis; Gratian's Decretum; secondary scholarship on canon law and demonology
